Mercari selected Chrome Enterprise Premium and Chromebooks to secure its highly sensitive customer service (CS) environment. Handling personally identifiable information (PII) on a daily basis, Mercari required a se
entries.content:
Yu Susaki

Manager of Enterprise Security, Mercari

Chrome Enterprise Premium

Add advanced security protections on top of streamlined management with Chrome Enterprise Premium.

Learn more

Editor's Note: Today's post is by Yu Susaki, Manager of Enterprise Security at Mercari, a leading consumer-to-consumer (C2C) marketplace with more than 20 million monthly active users. Mercari selected Chrome Enterprise Premium and Chromebooks to secure its highly sensitive customer service (CS) environment. Handling personally identifiable information (PII) on a daily basis, Mercari required a security strategy that could protect its data while addressing the operational inefficiencies and high costs of its legacy Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI). With a customer service environment largely driven by strategic partners, Mercari needed a scalable solution to empower agents to work securely and seamlessly while implementing safeguards to protect against data loss.

Flexibility and security with one secure enterprise browser

Previously, our customer service environment relied on a mix of legacy devices routed through VDI. This created operational friction, a frustrating user experience, increased IT overhead, and required managing overlapping DLP controls on both the VDI and local environments to prevent potential data transfer between the two. To simplify our architecture, we decided to shift focus from OS-level isolation to browser-layer data control, introducing Chrome Enterprise Premium and Chromebooks to a partner environment to establish data control and boundaries based on user actions.

By leveraging Chrome Enterprise Premium, our team configured strict DLP rules, implementing controls to restrict users from pasting or uploading files to destinations outside of Mercari's approved business tools. This helps protect sensitive company data from being leaked or fed into unapproved channels. We knew investing in Chrome Enterprise Premium would help enable AI-powered productivity while restricting data leaks to unsanctioned AI tools. The transition was smooth because our workforce was already using the Chrome Enterprise browser across the company prior to the security upgrade. Because employees were able to continue using the browser interface they were already accustomed to, the implementation of the new security solution was easier and resulted in strong user adoption. By implementing these policy controls, we could confidently adopt new AI capabilities while ensuring enterprise data boundaries are strictly enforced.

Beyond DLP, transitioning to this new architecture dramatically streamlined IT operations and reduced costs. With zero-touch enrollment, IT no longer needs to manually set up individual devices before handing them to users. Furthermore, by reducing dependency on VDI and consolidating various security agents (like legacy DLP, MDM, and EDR), we project a cost reduction of more than 50% over a three-year period within this environment, covering device costs, VDI running costs, and security licenses.

Additionally, this browser-centric model eliminates the heavy operational overhead and specialized engineering resources traditionally required just to maintain a complex VDI infrastructure, allowing us to redirect valuable IT talent to higher-priority initiatives.

Implementing Chrome Enterprise Premium and ChromeOS enabled a zero-trust, device-based approach that protects data, slashes IT costs, and measurably improves security. We eliminated VDI friction, lowered costs, and strictly enforced data boundaries—ultimately making Chrome Enterprise Premium the right move to deeply protect our marketplace and users.

Looking ahead, we are set up as an AI-forward organization that wants its employees to benefit from new technologies, like agentic browsers, but in a highly controlled environment. To achieve this, we leveraged the power of Chrome Enterprise Premium. As a first step, we are using browser policies to enable a safe, read-only adoption of Gemini in Chrome. Employees can now leverage multi-page context and seamless side-panel interactions without manual copy-pasting, which drastically reduces the risk of unintended actions like data modification. Looking forward, we plan to continuously explore the optimal balance between AI productivity and security. By dynamically utilizing both existing and upcoming enterprise security features alongside Chrome Enterprise Premium’s robust DLP, we will ensure data boundaries evolve proactively, empowering our workforce to innovate safely.

entries.title: How Nammu21 automates syndicated loans on Google Cloud Universal Ledger
entries.summary: The syndicated loan and private credit markets, both critical components of corporate finance, have long been constrained by manual processes, leading to multi-week settlements, valuation opacity, and trade friction. To solve these long-standing challenges, fintech innovator Nammu21 partnered with Google Cloud on a new proof-of-concept. Using its AI-powered platform to structure legal agreements a
entries.content:
Chang Yang Jiao

Head of Blockchain, Nammu21

Moritz Platt

Capital Markets Technology Manager

The syndicated loan and private credit markets, both critical components of corporate finance, have long been constrained by manual processes, leading to multi-week settlements, valuation opacity, and trade friction.

To solve these long-standing challenges, fintech innovator Nammu21 partnered with Google Cloud on a new proof-of-concept. Using its AI-powered platform to structure legal agreements and instantiate them as smart contracts on the Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL), Nammu21 automates the entire loan lifecycle, paving the way for improved settlement times and greater market efficiency.

Digitizing the loan market

While loan markets provide billions in capital to businesses worldwide, their underlying infrastructure has not kept pace with the speed of digital finance. This landscape requires continuous coordination across facility agents, borrowers, and diverse lender syndicates, while also managing highly customized credit agreements with dynamic tranches and complex covenants.

In particular, relying on fragmented, manual interpretation of legal text often results in significant operational drag and data silos. According to the Loan Market Association, secondary market settlement times for par/near par loans in Q4 2024 still averaged 42 days, with a median of 27 days. These notoriously slow timelines tie up capital, increase counterparty risk, and create a heavy reconciliation burden for participants.

Nammu21 transforms bespoke credit documents into programmable assets at scale by rendering each facility's governing terms as a Digital Credit Instrument (DCI). The DCI maps every term — including conditions, consents, eligibility criteria, and operational mechanics that determine what is permitted under a facility — directly back to its originating legal provision. These elements are then expressed as executable behaviours against a loan's live state.

To instantiate these instruments, the proof-of-concept utilizes the secure, high-performance execution environment of GCUL, an institutional-grade, permissioned distributed ledger that helps automate complex financial workflows to deliver near-instant transaction finality and predictable costs without the volatility or security concerns of public blockchains.

A purpose-built stack for digital credit

Combined with Nammu21’s data intelligence, GCUL provides the foundational infrastructure for converting legal document logic into live, programmable contracts. Designed to handle the privacy, scale, and multi-party coordination required by institutional finance, GCUL provides a permissioned, high-performance distributed ledger that delivers deterministic, instant transaction finality for high-value financial settlements.

Programmable contracts on GCUL are written in 

gculpy
, GCUL's domain-optimized programming language. As a strict, statically-typed subset of Python, 
gculpy
is designed to be safe, readable, and auditable, making it ideal for processing complex financial logic.

For regulated financial institutions, 

gculpy
offers distinct operational advantages over other ledger programming models. The language simplifies development by removing the need for complex memory management or workarounds to meet highly restrictive call stack limits, allowing engineers to focus on the financial logic itself. 

GCUL also provides robust, built-in permissioning, requiring explicit user authorization before a contract can store data on their behalf. This solves the "unsolicited asset" problem — common on public networks — where unwanted tokens can be sent to an organization's wallet, creating compliance and accounting issues. With GCUL, institutions can maintain full control over which assets they interact with to support their high-value, highly regulated use cases.

Nammu21 serves a dual role in this architecture. First, the platform renders the DCI programmatically from the original legal agreement without manual document reading to establish the terms. Next, it derives 

gculpy
contracts that define the structure of the obligation and govern the loan on GCUL, using the DCI to supply the terms that determine what the loan documents permit, require and block.

Technical architecture: The loan lifecycle on GCUL

Nammu21’s loan implementation on GCUL demonstrates the value of creating a single, immutable source of truth. The proof-of-concept modeled a $1.945 billion Term Loan B — one segment of a broader multi-facility transaction — where the agent bank, borrower, transferor, and transferee all worked off a permissioned view of the same on-ledger rendering.

The lifecycle begins when an agent bank selects a specific credit agreement transformed by Nammu21. The platform instantly provides the structured terms from the document, which are used to instantiate a unique 

gculpy
contract on GCUL, establishing a verifiable, on-ledger digital twin of that specific loan facility.

Next, the agent bank initiates the onboarding of the borrower and lenders. This multilateral action requires that each participant review the request and then provide explicit consent by approving the onboarding invitation from their own interface. Once all parties are onboarded, the agent bank records an immutable hash of the loan's key terms on-ledger, attesting that the on-ledger data matches the canonical off-ledger records.

Subsequent lifecycle events, such as secondary market transfers or repayments, are also managed as multi-step, automated workflows governed by a consent-driven model. For example, a transfer of a loan position requires new lender, borrower, and agent bank consent before it can be executed atomically on the ledger. All payment flows, from interest payments to loan close-outs, settle directly on GCUL using tokenized commercial bank money, eliminating the need for external payment rails.

Transacting with familiar, regulated money on a programmable ledger provides an architecture purpose-built for institutional finance, grounded in three core pillars:

1. Compliance via gated execution: Nammu21’s 

gculpy
contracts instantiated with governing terms, validate every action against the terms transformed from the agreement before execution, mitigating potential covenant breaches or invalid transfers upfront while eliminating the risk of silent failures. 

2. Role-based privacy: GCUL enforces strict, role-based access, ensuring that trading strategies, positions, and sensitive loan data remain confidential and are visible only to the necessary counterparties in a transaction.

3. Settlement finality: Every on-ledger action completes near-instantly and anchors on canonical data derived from the original credit agreement, replacing provisional, reconciliation-heavy models with real-time, trusted verification.

The business impact of moving on-ledger

This proof-of-concept illustrates a structural shift in how credit markets can operate. When each facility's governing terms are rendered as a DCI and executed on GCUL, the operational mechanics of lending markets change fundamentally, rather than incrementally.

Values can be reconciled bilaterally, but governance logic cannot – and the market’s current friction stems directly from each party's independent interpretation of the rules. Resolving this issue on-ledger is what enables settlement times to compress, back-office overhead to shrink, and counterparty risk to be mitigated by design rather than by manual checking.

This same architecture can be applied wherever credit terms are bespoke and manually interpreted. By freeing up capital that would otherwise be trapped in lengthy settlement cycles, new liquidity is unlocked and a more dynamic and efficient secondary loan market can emerge.

The team would also like to thank Someera Khokhar, Jordan Shelley, and Saskia A. Aalders at Nammu21 and Googlers Ishan Singh, Kathryn Stavish, Tom Chudy, and Stathis Onasoglou for their contributions.

entries.title: Leading in the agentic era: How to put people first as you adopt AI agents
entries.summary: Over the past few years, our Google Cloud Consulting team has partnered with many companies to introduce AI into their daily operations. In that time, we’ve seen the focus shift from generative AI that answers questions to agentic systems that fully carry out the work. These agents can create multi-step plans and manage a project from start to finish. While budget, compute, and tooling can help la
entries.content:
Christine Goglia

Agentic Transformation Lead, Google Cloud

Over the past few years, our Google Cloud Consulting team has partnered with many companies to introduce AI into their daily operations.

In that time, we’ve seen the focus shift from generative AI that answers questions to agentic systems that fully carry out the work. These agents can create multi-step plans and manage a project from start to finish.

While budget, compute, and tooling can help launch an agent program, enterprise adoption takes intentional culture work. People need to feel empowered enough to experiment with agents, and leaders need to show teams what agents mean for their roles.

Based on our work across these organizations, we’ve put together five practical lessons for guiding enterprises through an agentic shift.

1. Make workflows agent-executed, human-directed

Most enterprise workflows run like a relay race: one person completes a task, checks it, and hands it off to the next person, who then does the same. Layering an AI agent onto that model gives you a faster runner for one leg, but the handoffs may stall or slow down other work.

Redesigning your workflows can remove blockers like these in a few ways:

  • Strategic direction: Move from human-in-the-loop validation (where a person checks each step) to a human-in-the-lead model. Agents take on the work, and people set the direction and own the outcomes.

  • Parallel dependencies: One agent can handle every dependency at once instead of passing work through a multi-person queue. For example, an agent can check product availability, credit limits, and contract paperwork at the same time without waiting on each step to finish.

  • Manage by exception: Once the process is set up this way, the agent absorbs routine deterministic transactions, routing only ambiguous or high-judgment scenarios to human review. Cross-team stalls disappear, and your team stays in control.

2. Turn hesitation into ownership

In our experience, the biggest barrier to adoption is trust. Many employees worry about their value if an agent handles most of their day-to-day tasks. Others are concerned with who takes the blame if an agent makes a mistake. We encourage teams to treat agents the way they'd treat a junior team member:

  • Active delegation: Frame agents as digital coworkers. That means assigning tasks to them, defining their scope, and checking their work for accuracy.

  • Clear responsibilities: Set boundaries around which decisions an agent can make and which require human sign-off. When team members know exactly where accountability sits, they can better direct agents.

  • Comfort through exposure: Confidence grows through familiarity. We recommend starting with low-stakes use cases (like scheduling internal meetings) to help motivate teams before moving to high-stakes operations (such as financial forecasting).

3. Manage hybrid teams of people and agents

Next, it’s important to support collaboration when you bring agents into your team. Let’s look at how this might work in practice,

  • Focus on results: Collaborate across teams to break down workflows at both the tool and task level. Cross-functional perspectives reveal an end-to-end view of the process, helping you pinpoint where agentic capabilities belong and how to prioritize ideas by technical feasibility and business impact.

  • Reinforce behaviors: Top performers on a hybrid team are the people who guide their agents well. Reward team members for auditing an agent's reasoning and catching when its logic drifts from company goals.

  • Coach your teams: Show your teams how to work with agents so people can spend more time on creative work and decision-making.

4. Build agentic literacy through experimentation

Your teams need to understand how agents solve problems. People who know where an agent's logic breaks down (and why) can guide and judge its output.

  • Beyond the tool: Literacy covers both writing a good prompt and auditing the result. Agents choose the most likely path instead of following deterministic rules, so people need to know when to trust an agent's output and when to check it.

  • Safe learning zones: Give business roles the same sandbox access that technical teams get to build agentic literacy across the whole organization.

  • Celebrating intelligent failure: Experimentation is how teams learn. In our experience, we’ve seen that when teams build an agent that fails because the data wasn't accurate, that team then understands how important data readiness is. Even if it didn’t work out, this should still be encouraged so your teams keep experimenting.

5. Govern agents with a hub-and-spoke model

To roll agents out across an enterprise, you need central guardrails that don't slow down the teams closest to the work. A hub-and-spoke model does both: it gives teams a shared foundation to build on and room to move at their own pace.

  • The hub: Establish a central AI council team that sets guidelines, maintains ethical guardrails, and manages a library of approved tools. That way, teams don't rebuild the same things.

  • The spokes: Allow individual teams to adapt those tools to their own needs, experiment quickly, and give feedback on what works in practice.

Within Google Cloud Consulting, we use our internal Agent Catalog to share low-code agents and skills that drive cross-team learning, innovation, and efficiency. However, you don’t need to build a custom platform to implement this. Here are a few approaches:

  • Filter and sort agents made by employees through a simple internal web app.

  • Publish and share agents with built-in Gemini Enterprise features like Agent Gallery.

  • Work directly with technical teams that help organizations create tailored solutions.

Lead with a people-first approach to AI

Becoming an agentic organization is about your people. Give your teams systems and guardrails to move fast, room to experiment, and leadership that promotes accountability.

Ultimately, the overarching goal is to build an organization where human ingenuity and agents support and amplify one another.

Get started

  • Explore free courses on Google Skills: Build in-demand AI expertise at your own pace and guide your teams through the agentic journey.

  • Join a Build with Gemini workshop: Sign up today to discover hands-on strategies for creating agentic literacy and empowering your teams to lead with AI.

entries.title: Five rules for evaluating agent skills before they bloat your context window
entries.summary: You’re probably hearing more about SKILL.md files, and you’ll see that a lot of people test them the same way: paste a prompt into chat, watch it pass once on a laptop, and merge to main. But when you paste three pages of CLI docs into a markdown file without an evaluation loop, you are just as likely to confuse a frontier model as you are to help it. For the past weeks, we have been diligently me
entries.content:
Karl Weinmeister

Director, Developer Relations

Alan Blount

Product Manager

You’re probably hearing more about SKILL.md files, and you’ll see that a lot of people test them the same way: paste a prompt into chat, watch it pass once on a laptop, and merge to main. But when you paste three pages of CLI docs into a markdown file without an evaluation loop, you are just as likely to confuse a frontier model as you are to help it.

For the past weeks, we have been diligently measuring and optimizing our own Google Cloud Developer Plugin, with the most essential skills and the Developer Knowledge MCP server to ground responses in the documentation.

We ran dozens of scenarios with Gemini, Antigravity, and other agents. We used Claude Sonnet 5 on Gemini platform inside isolated Harbor pods on GKE Autopilot. And, we contributed Kubernetes and Gemini platform capabilities upstream to NVIDIA's open-source evaluator. 

Here's the five-rule engineering playbook we use to verify a skill is worth its tokens.

1. Gate trigger collisions and security risks before spinning up containers

When an evaluation run shows zero improvement between your plugin arm and your baseline arm (Δ = 0), the natural urge is to rewrite the body of your SKILL.md instructions. Hold off on that. Nine times out of ten, the agent never loaded your skill in the first place.

Coding agents do not read full SKILL.md bodies at turn zero. The router only inspects the short name and description in your YAML frontmatter. Once a workspace grows past a dozen skills, two failure modes collide: under-triggering (your description describes internal implementation rather than developer intent) and sibling hijacking (a broad phrase like "helps with cloud deployments" in a neighboring skill intercepts the prompt first).

We recently open-sourced skill-reach so you can catch frontmatter collisions before spending on container sandboxes. It validates manifests, computes vocabulary overlap against nearest rival skills, and runs empirical routing probes across Claude Code, Google Antigravity, and OpenAI Codex:

Pair skill-reach with NVIDIA's SkillSpector (Tier 1 and Tier 2 of SkillEvaluator). As the Nemotron Labs team details in their Evaluating Agent Skills deep dive, standard code linters miss agent-native risks buried in markdown prose: prompt injection, silent data exfiltration, tool poisoning, and trigger abuse. 

2. Never trust an eval that runs on a developer laptop

If you run skill benchmarks directly on your workstation, your numbers are lying to you. A developer laptop is packed with ambient state that contaminates the baseline arm:

  • Cached Google Cloud credentials

  • Exported project variables and warm bash history

  • Global environment rules

An unassisted baseline agent can pass a cloud deployment test by inheriting a default project ID or token sitting in your local shell profile, masking the exact failure your skill was written to solve.

Host resource contention also warps agent trajectories. While hill climbing code-retrieval agents with AlphaEvolve, our internal testing showed that running the exact same agent benchmark while a workstation was under CPU load dropped the score. Slower file scans and subprocess timeouts cause the agent to abandon search paths prematurely.

3. Measure paired WITH vs. W/OUT ablation (Pass@3), not vibes

Running prompts a single time and screenshotting the green checkmarks is not a real evaluation. Multi-turn tool-using agents branch on every shell exit code and stdout snippet. In our retrieval study, more than a third of benchmark tasks produced different scores across consecutive runs of the exact same code and prompt.

A perfect score is equally meaningless without a paired baseline for comparison. Both Claude's plugin eval tool and NVIDIA's SkillEvaluator run paired ablation across multiple repetitions: Arm A runs the base model in a clean sandbox without the skill, while Arm B runs the identical prompt and sandbox with the skill mounted.

Comparing the score improvements across our sandbox trials exposed three clear patterns that single-shot testing hides. Without the plugin, the base model still stumbled into a working deployment on most runs, but only after burning minutes of wall-clock time guessing deprecated flags and retrying bad requests. Conversely, when a test case shows identical success with zero efficiency gain, the base model already owns that capability natively. Your skill is pure context tax — delete it.

4. Separate efficiency and security from correctness so agents can't reward-hack

When you connect an evaluation harness to an automated optimizer (like AlphaEvolve or reach optimize), it is a surprisingly common pattern for the agent to cheat the grader.

In our AlphaEvolve retrieval experiments, evolved candidates discovered four distinct ways to game the benchmark without solving the task. When the grading harness blocked specific expected substring checks in source code, an evolved candidate dynamically concatenated strings at runtime, traversed up the directory tree, and read the ground-truth answer file directly off disk. Another candidate spawned subprocesses to bypass AST checks.

The evolutionary loop favored those cheaters because the fitness formula blended correctness (0.95 weight) and token efficiency (0.05 weight) into a single score. Reading the answer file from disk takes no LLM turns, earning an efficiency bonus that gives cheaters a survival advantage over honest agents that spent tokens searching the repository.

Hardening your skill evaluator against reward-hacking takes three structural guardrails. First, configure Harbor so your test fixtures, grading scripts, and answer keys live inside a dedicated verifier container that mounts workspace artifacts only after the agent container exits. Second, keep SkillEvaluator's five dimensions (Correctness, Discoverability, Efficiency, Effectiveness, and Security) strictly orthogonal; never let token thrift compensate for a failed test or a security violation. Third, in NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator#140, we extended security checks to fail any trial that reads Kubernetes service account tokens or queries cloud metadata endpoints, while redacting live OAuth tokens from saved trajectories.

5. Encode operational habits, not documentation dumps

Looking across all of our trials, the difference between the skills that delivered a score improvement in our sandbox benchmark and the community skills that failed came down to what was inside the markdown.

Skills that copy-paste public API reference tables into skill files yield almost no lift. Frontier models already have public cloud docs in their pretraining weights; dumping thousands of words of static flags into the prompt just inflates time-to-first-token and buries actionable constraints.

The skills that increased our Efficiency score in our test suite taught compact operational habits and verification reflexes instead of encyclopedic reference text:

  • Verify CLI flags at the leaf subcommand before mutating state: Rather than listing dozens of flags in markdown, the skill teaches a simple reflex: verify help output at the command line before executing a state-changing deployment.

  • Route through a lightweight catalog index on demand: Rather than loading fourteen heavy cloud skills into context at once, a thin root router checks a curated remote index and pulls only the specific recipe needed for the task.

  • Enforce least-privilege auth defaults: Explicit guardrails instruct agents to authenticate via Application Default Credentials rather than downloading static service-account JSON keys, while enforcing unauthenticated access restrictions alongside explicit invoker IAM bindings.

Because our evaluation stack runs in CI, upgrading models takes one flag change. We re-run the paired WITH vs. W/OUT matrix against the new model and delete every skill whose Delta drops to zero. Deleting a skill because the new model graduated past it is one of the cleanest high-fives in software engineering.
